subtitle: An index and brief summary of 100 RFCs covering a span of Internet standards.

tldr.problem: Readers need to know what RFCs 2700 through 2799 cover to find relevant specifications.

facts.label: Format

today: RFC 2799 is an Informational RFC that serves as a historical index. RFCs continue to be published, and newer summary indexes exist for more recent RFC ranges (e.g., RFC 3000 for the 2900-2999 range). The authoritative source for all RFC statuses is the current edition of RFC 2700 (or its successors), maintained by IANA.

sections.title: Purpose of the RFC Summary
sections.content:
RFC 2799 is a periodic index memo summarizing the 100 RFCs numbered 2700 through 2799, published in September 2000. It is fundamentally a bookkeeping document—its purpose is to provide readers with a snapshot of what RFCs exist in this range, when they were published, who authored them, and what they are about.

This document is not a protocol specification and does not introduce new standards. Instead, it serves as an aid for researchers, engineers, and operators who want an overview of standardization work in this range. Some of the listed RFCs are on the standards track (progressing toward becoming official Internet Standards), while others are informational or experimental.
sections.eli5: When you have a big section of an encyclopedia with 100 articles, you want a page that lists the title and topic of each one so you know what to read.

sections.title: Scope and Organization
sections.content:
This RFC covers all RFCs from 2700 through 2799 inclusive. The RFCs are listed in descending order (from 2799 down to 2700), with each entry showing the RFC number, author, date, title, and a single-paragraph description of the document's scope and status.

Each summary is brief—typically one or two sentences. The RFC notes that many of these documents are on the standards track, meaning they are either Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or Standards. However, the status of RFCs can change over time, so this document should not be treated as the authoritative source for current RFC status; instead, readers are directed to the current edition of "Internet Official Protocol Standards" (RFC 2700) for authoritative status.
sections.eli5: The list goes from the newest to the oldest, and for each one it just tells you what it is in one sentence.

sections.title: Topics in RFCs 2700-2799
sections.content: The RFCs in this range cover a diverse set of Internet topics. Major categories include: Network protocols and routing (BGP, IS-IS, OSPF enhancements, IP tunneling, multicast); Transport and application protocols (DNS extensions, HTTP, FTP security); Security and authentication (Kerberos for TLS, certificate management, RSVP security); Quality of Service and policy (RSVP extensions, COPS, admission control); Management protocols (SNMP, MIB definitions for various services); Infrastructure and encoding (IPv6, IPv4/IPv6 translation, UTF-16, Dublin Core metadata); Multimedia (RTP payload formats, text conversation over RTP); System administration (LDAP, vCard extensions, Host Resources MIB).
sections.eli5: The 100 RFCs in this batch cover lots of different topics: routing, security, quality of service, management, and multimedia.

sections.title: Standards-Track versus Other RFCs
sections.content:
Within this range, some RFCs are marked as Standards-Track (progressing through Proposed, Draft, and Standard status), while others are Informational (providing information without attempting to standardize) or Experimental (describing early-stage ideas). The RFC notes that the status is not static—an RFC might start as Proposed Standard and later advance to Draft Standard or Standard, or it might be proposed but never progress.

This memo emphasizes that for the definitive current status of any RFC, readers should consult RFC 2700 (Internet Official Protocol Standards), which is the authoritative list maintained by IANA and IETF. RFC 2799 serves only as a convenient index and summary guide to the range.
sections.eli5: Some of these are official standards approved by IETF, some are just proposals, and some are experimental. Check RFC 2700 to be sure which ones are official.

sections.title: Using This Index
sections.content:
This RFC is designed to be browsed by engineers and operators who want to get a sense of the standards activity in a particular RFC range. Readers scanning through this list might discover related work they were not previously aware of, or they might verify that a particular specification falls within this range and verify its status without needing to look up each RFC individually.

For specific protocol details, readers should consult the actual RFCs themselves. This index is a convenience tool for discovery and overview, not a substitute for reading the full specifications.
sections.eli5: If you're building a network and want to know if there's an RFC about IPv6, DNS, or management in this batch, you can scan this list without reading all 100 RFCs.

references.text: Reynolds, J., "Internet Official Protocol Standards", RFC 2700, August 2000.
